hero.title: Waist-to-Height Ratio
hero.lead:
Keep your waist measurement to less than half your height. That is the entire rule, it needs nothing but a tape measure, and it captures something the bathroom scale genuinely cannot: where your body is storing fat, rather than just how much you weigh.

Waist-to-height ratio has quietly become one of the measures health services recommend alongside — and sometimes ahead of — BMI, because fat carried around the middle behaves very differently from fat carried elsewhere. This guide covers the 0.5 threshold, how to measure your waist so the number means something, target sizes for every height, and why the two measurements work best as a pair.

sections.heading: The 0.5 rule
sections.html:
Divide your waist measurement by your height, in the same units. A waist of 84 cm at a height of 175 cm gives 84 ÷ 175 = 0.48. In inches it works identically: a 33-inch waist at 69 inches tall is 33 ÷ 69 = 0.48. Same answer, because it is a ratio.

RatioCategoryWhat it suggests
Below 0.4Possibly too lowWorth checking with a doctor, especially if unintentional
0.4 – 0.49HealthyCentral fat in a range associated with lowest risk
0.5 – 0.59Increased riskA useful prompt to act, not a diagnosis
0.6 and aboveHigh riskWorth discussing with your doctor

What makes the rule unusually good is how few exceptions it needs. The same 0.5 threshold applies to men and women, to most ethnic groups, and to children from about age five — where BMI needs sex-specific ranges, ethnicity-adjusted cutoffs, and separate percentile charts for children. One number, one threshold, one tape measure.

The threshold is a screening prompt rather than a verdict. Crossing 0.5 does not mean something is wrong; it means the question is worth asking, ideally alongside blood pressure, blood sugar, and cholesterol at your next check-up.

sections.heading: How to measure your waist correctly
sections.html:
Almost all the error in this measurement comes from measuring in the wrong place or pulling the tape too hard. Ninety seconds of care gives you a number you can compare month to month.

  1. Bare skin or a single thin layer. Over a sweater is not a measurement.
  2. Find the right level. Midway between the bottom of your lowest rib and the top of your hip bone. Feel for both with your fingers — for many people this lands at or just above the navel, but the landmarks are what matter, not the belly button.
  3. Stand normally. Feet about hip-width apart, weight even, arms relaxed at your sides. Do not suck in.
  4. Breathe out naturally, then measure. Not a forced exhale — just the end of a normal breath.
  5. Keep the tape level. Check in a mirror that it sits horizontally all the way around, including at the back, where it tends to ride up.
  6. Snug, not tight. The tape should sit against the skin without compressing it. If it leaves a mark, ease off.
  7. Measure twice. If the two readings differ by more than a centimeter, take a third and use the middle one.

The mistakes that skew the number

  • Using your trouser size. Clothing waist sizes commonly run one to two inches smaller than the actual measurement, and vary by brand. Use a tape.
  • Measuring at the hips. The widest point around the hips is a different measurement entirely and will make the ratio look better than it is.
  • Inconsistent timing. Waist can vary by a couple of centimeters across a day with meals and bloating. Morning, before eating, is the most repeatable moment — the same logic behind consistent weigh-in timing.

You may also have seen fixed waist thresholds — around 94 cm (37 in) for men and 80 cm (31.5 in) for women. Those are still in use and still useful, but they ignore height entirely, which is unkind to short people and generous to tall ones. The ratio scales properly, which is why it has been gaining ground.

sections.heading: Why it complements BMI rather than replacing it
sections.html:
BMI and waist-to-height ratio answer different questions. BMI asks how heavy you are for your height. The ratio asks where that mass sits. Neither is redundant, and the interesting information appears when they disagree.

  • Normal BMI, high ratio. The case BMI misses most often — sometimes called normal-weight central obesity. Someone at BMI 23 with a waist over half their height is carrying visceral fat around the organs despite a reassuring weight. Visceral fat is the kind most strongly associated with type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, and heart disease, so this combination genuinely matters.
  • High BMI, healthy ratio. Common in muscular people. A BMI of 27 with a waist well under half your height usually means the extra weight is muscle, not fat — exactly the scenario where BMI alone is misleading.
  • Both healthy. Strong reassurance. Two independent measures agreeing is far more convincing than either alone.
  • Both raised. A clear prompt to talk to your doctor and look at the modifiable things: activity, sleep, alcohol, and diet.

The ratio also has one practical advantage over the scale: it moves in a way that feels fair. Increased activity tends to reduce visceral fat relatively early, so a waist can shrink noticeably in a period when body weight barely budges — because muscle is being added as fat comes off. If the scale has stalled but your waist is still falling, you are progressing, whatever the number says. For the fullest picture, add an estimate of body fat percentage, and check your weight against the range for your height in healthy weight for your height.

sections.heading: Keeping a record: tape and notebook vs app
sections.html:
Measure once and you have a snapshot. Measure monthly for a year and you have something genuinely informative — and a notebook does that job perfectly. A date and a number, twelve lines a year. There is nothing wrong with it, and a tape measure costs almost nothing.

The gap shows up when you want to see your waist next to your weight over the same period, which is where the useful story lives: the months where weight flattened but the waist kept coming down, or the reverse. Lining up two handwritten columns and reading a trend out of them is more work than anyone actually does.

The free Weight & BMI Feeltracker app keeps that history for you. It logs weight in kilograms or pounds, calculates BMI automatically, records body fat percentage, and lets you attach notes and photos to any entry — so a monthly waist measurement can live right beside the weigh-in it belongs to. Charts and trend lines cover any period you like, goal tracking shows how far you have come, reminders keep the habit alive, and everything syncs across iPhone, iPad, and Mac through iCloud with no account and no email address required. It syncs with Apple Health, and exports to PDF, XLSX, CSV, or JSON when you want to take something to a doctor. AI insights can summarize your own history, free to try, with more depth as an optional premium feature.

Either way, the tape measure is doing the real work. Keep it in the same drawer as the scale, and use it on the first of the month.

items.question: What is a healthy waist-to-height ratio?
items.answer: Below **0.5** — your waist should measure less than half your height. A ratio between 0.4 and 0.49 is the healthy band; 0.5 to 0.59 suggests increased risk, and 0.6 or above is worth discussing with your doctor.

items.question: Is waist-to-height ratio better than BMI?
items.answer: It is better at one specific thing: spotting fat stored around the organs, which [BMI](/weight/bmi-chart/) cannot see at all. But BMI is quicker, universally understood, and better validated for population screening. Use both — they disagree in informative ways.

items.question: Where exactly should I measure my waist?
items.answer: Midway between the bottom of your lowest rib and the top of your hip bone, on bare skin, standing normally, after breathing out. For many people that is at or just above the navel, but find the landmarks by feel rather than assuming.

items.question: Does the 0.5 rule apply to men and women equally?
items.answer: Yes, which is one of its main advantages. The same threshold works for both sexes, across most ethnic groups, and for children from around age five — no separate charts or adjusted cutoffs needed.

items.question: How often should I measure my waist?
items.answer: Monthly is ideal. Waist changes slowly, and measuring more often mostly captures day-to-day bloating rather than real change. Measure in the morning before eating, and always with the same technique.

data.disclaimerText: This article is for general information only and is not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Waist-to-height ratio is a screening prompt, not a diagnosis, and cannot assess your health on its own — always discuss your results, and any plan to change your weight, with your doctor or healthcare provider. Seek medical advice if your waist is increasing without a change in weight, if you are losing weight without trying, or if abdominal swelling comes with pain, persistent bloating, or changes in bowel habits.
